L:stability-triangle:3: - The **combined centre of gravity** of the forklift and load must stay **inside the stability triangle**.
L:stability-triangle:4: - If it moves outside, the forklift tips.
L:stability-triangle:6: - **Overloading** — lifting more than the rated capacity
L:stability-triangle:7: - **Lifting high** — raises the centre of gravity
L:stability-triangle:11: - **Ground giving way** — soft, backfilled or deteriorating ground
L:stability-triangle:13: - **Picking up or placing loads** carelessly — e.g. catching a rack, dropping a load
L:stability-triangle:14: - **Restricted spaces** that force tight turns or awkward approaches
L:stability-triangle:16: That's why you **travel with the load low and tilted back**, turn slowly, and never turn on a slope.
T:load-charts: The data plate and rated capacity
L:load-charts:1: Every forklift has a manufacturer's **data plate**. It shows the forklift's **rated capacity** — the **maximum weight it can safely lift**.
L:load-charts:2: > **Never lift more than the rated capacity.** If the load is heavier, don't lift it.
L:load-charts:3: The data plate also shows the **load centre** the capacity is rated at. The most common is **600 mm**.
L:load-charts:4: - **Load centre** — the distance from the vertical face of the tynes to the load's centre of gravity (the middle of its weight).
L:load-charts:5: - The rated capacity applies when the load centre is **no more than** the one on the data plate. If a load's centre of gravity is **further out** than that (for example a long crate), **don't lift it** — ask your supervisor.
L:load-charts:6: - **Attachments** — when an attachment is fitted, use the data plate for that attachment.
L:load-charts:8: Forklift A's data plate says **2,500 kg at a 600 mm load centre**. A pallet weighing **1,900 kg** with its load centre at **600 mm** is within capacity — **OK to lift**. A machine weighing **2,700 kg** is **200 kg over** — **don't lift it**.
L:load-charts:9: > Never add extra counterweight or put people on the back to "balance" a load.
L:load-charts:10: Only use attachments and modifications **approved by the manufacturer**, with a matching data plate.
T:working-out-load-weight: Working out the weight of a load
L:working-out-load-weight:0: ## Know the weight before you lift
L:working-out-load-weight:1: You can't check the load against the rated capacity if you don't know the weight. Ways to find it:
L:working-out-load-weight:2: - **Load labels and markings** on the item or pallet
L:working-out-load-weight:3: - **Consignment notes** and **running sheets** from the transport company
L:working-out-load-weight:5: - **Manufacturer's documentation** (e.g. for a machine or tank)
L:working-out-load-weight:6: - **The data plate** on equipment being moved (many machines show their own weight)
L:working-out-load-weight:7: - **Weighing** — weigh one carton and multiply, or use scales / a load-weighing indicator on the forklift
L:working-out-load-weight:8: If you can't confirm the weight — **don't lift it**. Ask your supervisor.
L:working-out-load-weight:10: **Total weight = (number of cartons × weight of one carton) + weight of the pallet**
L:working-out-load-weight:12: A pallet holds **5 layers of 8 cartons**. Each carton weighs **20 kg**. The pallet weighs **25 kg**.
L:working-out-load-weight:16: Then compare it with the forklift's **rated capacity** on the data plate. If 825 kg is less than or equal to the rated capacity, it's OK to lift.
L:working-out-load-weight:17: > **Count → Multiply → Add the pallet.** Use a calculator and write each step down — that's what you'll do in the assessment too.
L:attachments:1: An attachment **adds weight** to the front of the forklift and usually **moves the load centre forward**. Both reduce how much you can safely lift.
L:attachments:2: - Only fit attachments **approved by the manufacturer** for that forklift.
L:attachments:3: - The forklift must have a **data plate that covers the attachment**.
L:attachments:4: - Check the attachment is **secured** (locking pins, bolts, hydraulic connections) before use.
L:attachments:7:
| Attachment | Used for | Key safety points |
|---|---|---|
| **Side shifter** | Moving the tynes sideways to line up loads | Centre the load before travelling |
| **Fork extensions (slippers)** | Long or deep loads | Must be rated and the right size for the tynes, fully secured; capacity reduces |
| **Jib** | Lifting a load from a hook | The suspended load **swings** — move slowly; capacity varies by hook position |
| **Carpet spike / pole** | Carpet rolls, coils | Insert fully; watch for loads sliding off |
| **Drum carrier / clamp** | Drums | Drum must be gripped securely; liquids can slosh |
| **Bale clamp** | Bales (wool, cotton, hay, paper) | Correct clamp pressure — too little drops it, too much damages it |
| **Paper roll clamp** | Large paper rolls | Correct clamp pressure; rolls are heavy for their size |
| **Rotator** | Rotating or tipping loads | Rotating shifts the centre of gravity — rotate with the load low and the forklift stationary |
| **Personnel (work) platform** | Lifting people to work at height | Only a purpose-built platform designed for the forklift, secured to it, with the operator at the controls. **Never** lift people on the tynes or a pallet. |
L:unusual-loads:1: If the weight isn't centred, the centre of gravity shifts **sideways** and the forklift is easier to tip in a turn.
L:unusual-loads:2: - Position the tynes so the load is **centred** between them — use the side shift if fitted.
L:unusual-loads:3: - If a load is badly stacked, have it **restacked** before lifting.
L:unusual-loads:5: Long, wide, tall or odd-shaped loads (pipes, timber, machinery):
L:unusual-loads:6: - Spread the tynes **as wide as practical** for the load.
L:unusual-loads:7: - Allow **extra clearance** — long loads swing wide on turns.
L:unusual-loads:8: - Use an **observer** if the load blocks your view.
L:unusual-loads:11: A **dynamic load** moves while you're carrying it — liquids in drums or IBCs, or a load hanging from a jib. The movement adds force and shifts the centre of gravity.
L:unusual-loads:14: - Avoid sudden stops — a swinging load keeps moving.
L:unusual-loads:16: Use **gluts or dunnage** (timber blocks or bearers) under loads so the tynes can be inserted and withdrawn without damaging the load.
T:weights-and-quantities: Load weights: units, totals and maximum quantities
L:weights-and-quantities:1: Every load calculation uses the same few steps. Take it slowly, **use a calculator**, and **write each step down**.
L:weights-and-quantities:4: Rated capacity on the data plate is in **kilograms (kg)**. Paperwork sometimes uses **tonnes (t)**.
L:weights-and-quantities:5: **1 tonne = 1,000 kg.** To change tonnes into kilograms, **multiply by 1,000**.
L:weights-and-quantities:8: When a pallet has different items on it, **add every item, then add the pallet**.
L:weights-and-quantities:9:
> A pallet weighing **50 kg** carries items of **400 kg**, **350 kg** and **600 kg**.
> 400 + 350 + 600 = 1,350 kg → add the pallet: 1,350 + 50 = **1,400 kg**
L:weights-and-quantities:12: 2. **Multiply:** number of cartons × weight of one carton
L:weights-and-quantities:14:
> 5 layers of 10 cartons, 20 kg each, on a 30 kg pallet:
> 5 × 10 = 50 cartons → 50 × 20 = 1,000 kg → 1,000 + 30 = **1,030 kg**
L:weights-and-quantities:16: A weighbridge weighs the whole truck. **Load = loaded truck − empty truck.**
L:weights-and-quantities:17:
> Loaded truck **18,000 kg**, empty truck **12,000 kg** → load = **6,000 kg**.
> If that's **4 identical pallets**: 6,000 ÷ 4 = **1,500 kg each**.
L:weights-and-quantities:18: ## The most cartons you can carry
L:weights-and-quantities:19: 1. Take the pallet off the limit: **limit − pallet**
L:weights-and-quantities:20: 2. Divide by the weight of one carton
L:weights-and-quantities:21: 3. If the answer has a decimal, **round DOWN** — never up
L:weights-and-quantities:22:
> Limit **1,000 kg**, pallet **20 kg**, cartons **30 kg** each:
> 1,000 − 20 = 980 → 980 ÷ 30 = 32.67 → **32 cartons**.
> Check: 33 cartons would be 33 × 30 + 20 = **1,010 kg** — over the limit.
L:working-out-load-centre:1: The **load centre** is the distance from the **front face of the tynes** (where the load sits against the backrest) to the **middle of the load's weight** (its centre of gravity).
L:working-out-load-centre:2: Most forklift data plates are rated at a **600 mm** load centre.
L:working-out-load-centre:3: ## Even loads pushed hard against the backrest
L:working-out-load-centre:4: If the weight is spread evenly, the centre of gravity is in the **middle** of the load.
L:working-out-load-centre:5: **Load centre = depth of the load ÷ 2** (half the depth)
